input.essay:
Allied wartime promises and the peace settlements changed political authority in the Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire a great deal, but mostly by replacing Ottoman rule with European control instead of giving the Arabs the independence they had been promised. The documents show that Britain and France made promises that did not match each other, and in the end the European powers kept the real power.

The First World War put the Ottoman Empire on the side of the Central Powers, which made its Arab lands a target for Britain and France.

Document 1 shows what Arab leaders wanted. Hussein, the Sharif of Mecca, asks Britain to acknowledge the independence of the Arab countries within borders he lists, and also to approve an Arab Khalifate of Islam. Hussein says the whole Arab nation has decided to be free, but he was writing in 1915 as a ruler who wanted British help against the Ottomans, so this claim to speak for everyone was partly a way to get a better deal. It shows that Arab leaders expected to hold power themselves once the Ottomans were gone.

Document 3, the Sykes-Picot Agreement, shows that Britain and France were planning something different. It says they will recognize independent Arab states or a confederation, but France and Britain would have priority in their own areas, would supply the advisers, and could set up direct or indirect administration and control in the blue and red areas. This was an agreement between two European governments, and it was kept secret until Russia's revolutionary government published it in 1917. The secrecy matters because it meant Hussein was being promised independence while the two powers were quietly dividing up influence, so the Arabs were not told the truth. This makes the idea of Arab independence in the agreement look more like a cover than a real plan.

Document 6, Article 22 of the League of Nations Covenant, shows the final result. Territories that had left Ottoman rule were to be placed under the tutelage of advanced nations as Mandatories. The document says this is a sacred trust and says some former Turkish communities could be provisionally recognized as independent nations with advice from a Mandatory. The language is paternalistic, since it says these peoples are not yet able to stand by themselves, and it was written by the victorious powers at the peace conference, not by Arabs. So the settlement put European states in charge under a polite name.

Overall, political authority was reshaped because Ottoman sovereignty ended and Britain and France took over, but it was not reshaped in the way Hussein asked for in Document 1. The promises of independence were followed by secret zones and then mandates, so the change mostly meant one outside power was replaced by others.

Industrialization changed the relationships between industrial and non-industrial societies more deeply than it changed conditions inside industrial societies. Life in Britain changed a lot, but the biggest shift was in power, because industrial states like Britain were able to force their will on countries that had not industrialized.

Inside industrial societies, work and daily life changed. Adam Smith, writing in 1776, describes a pin factory where the work is divided into about eighteen distinct operations, so that each worker does one small job. This shows that machines and the division of labor made production much faster, since a worker alone could hardly make one pin a day. Smith was a Scottish economist who was writing to explain how nations get wealthy, so he focuses on the benefits of production and does not talk about how the workers felt. Because of his purpose, his document shows the gains of industry but leaves out its costs. Friedrich Engels shows the other side. He says the steam engine and cotton machinery created the proletariat in England and altered the whole of society. Engels was a German who helped run his family's cotton business in Manchester, so he saw the factory system up close, and that makes his account believable. At the same time, he was a critic of capitalism who wanted to expose the working class's suffering, so he may have picked the worst examples. Together these two documents show that industrialization raised production while creating a new working class that often lived badly. Parliament eventually responded with the Factory Act of 1833, which limited child labor in textile mills, showing that the problems inside Britain were serious enough that the government had to act.

The relationship between industrial and non-industrial societies changed even more. In 1793 the Qianlong Emperor told King George III that China possessed all things and had no use for British manufactures. At that time China could simply refuse what Britain wanted. By 1858, after the Second Opium War, the Treaty of Tientsin said that British subjects in China would be tried under British law by their own consul. This is a huge change, because China no longer controlled justice on its own land. This shows that industrial power gave Britain the strength to turn trade requests into demands.

In conclusion, industrialization changed both kinds of relationships, but the shift between countries was more dramatic. Inside Britain, people still worked, lived in cities and were governed by the same state, though conditions changed. Between Britain and China, the situation was almost reversed from 1793 to 1858.

input.essay:
Before 1750, most goods in the world were made by hand in homes or small workshops, and Asia, especially China and India, produced a large share of the world's manufactured goods like silk, porcelain and cotton cloth. Britain was mainly a trading nation, and the British East India Company bought tea from China and cotton textiles from India, often paying in silver because Europeans had few goods Asians wanted. When steam engines and the factory system spread in Britain in the late 1700s, this balance began to shift. Industrialization greatly changed conditions inside industrial societies by raising production while creating a new working class living in crowded cities, but it changed the relationships between industrial and non-industrial societies even more, turning China and India from powerful producers into markets that were forced open and kept dependent.

Inside industrial societies, the first big change was in how work was organized. Adam Smith describes a pin factory where making a pin is "divided into about eighteen distinct operations," so that workers make far more pins than one man alone could make (Doc 1). Smith was writing in 1776, before most of the Industrial Revolution, and as an economist who supported free markets his purpose was to show the benefits of the division of labor, so he focuses on productivity and says little about how the workers felt. Later writers saw the costs. Friedrich Engels says the steam engine and cotton machinery created "an industrial revolution" that "altered the whole civil society" and produced the proletariat (Doc 3). Because Engels was a German who helped manage his family's cotton business in Manchester, he saw factory life up close, which makes his account believable, but he was also a socialist critic who wanted to prove that capitalism created a suffering class, so he chose England as the "classic" example to support his argument. Gustave Dore's engraving of London shows rows of cramped brick houses with tiny yards packed with people, and a railway with a smoking train running over them (Doc 5). Dore was an artist making a dramatic book, so he may have exaggerated how dark and crowded it was, but the picture still shows that railways and industry made cities grow quickly without good housing. These problems led to reforms like the Factory Act of 1833 in Britain, which limited child labor in textile mills, showing that industrial societies had to change their laws to deal with the conditions industry created.

The change in relationships between societies was even larger. In 1793 the Qianlong Emperor told George III that China possessed "all things" and had "no use for your country's manufactures" (Doc 2). Since he was writing to a foreign king to refuse a request, he wanted to show Chinese superiority within the tribute system, and at that time China really was strong. By 1858 things were very different. After losing the Opium Wars, China signed the Treaty of Tientsin, which said British subjects who committed crimes in China would be tried "according to the Laws of Great Britain" (Doc 4). This extraterritoriality shows that industrial military power let Britain ignore Chinese law. By 1922 Sun Yat-sen describes China as the "dumping ground" for Western over-production with a trade imbalance of over a hundred million dollars a year (Doc 7). Sun was trying to attract foreign investment, so he presents China as an opportunity for the West, but he still admits China's weak position.

However, this change was not simply accepted. Gandhi argued that machinery "represents a great sin" and that Bombay mill workers had "become slaves" (Doc 6). As an Indian nationalist he wanted to reject Western civilization, yet he still admits Indians were buying "Manchester cloth," which shows how dependent India had become. Sun, on the other hand, wanted China to industrialize. So non-industrial societies both resisted industrialization and tried to copy it, which shows that its effects on relationships were deep but contested.

Before World War I, the Arab provinces were ruled by the Ottoman Empire, but in the early 1900s the Young Turks tried to centralize the empire and push Turkish language and control, which made many Arabs resent Ottoman rule. Small Arab nationalist groups started to form and wanted more self-rule. When the Ottomans joined the war on the side of Germany in 1914, Britain needed allies against them in the Middle East, and Britain and France were also rivals who both wanted influence in the region for trade and strategy. This mix of Arab nationalism and European imperial competition set up the promises made during the war. Between 1915 and 1922, Allied commitments and the peace settlement greatly reshaped political authority by ending Ottoman rule and creating new territories, but they mostly replaced one outside power with another, because Britain made contradictory promises and in the end put its own and France's interests ahead of Arab independence.

At first, it looked like the Arabs would gain real independence. In Document 1, Hussein asks England to "acknowledge the independence of the Arab countries" over a huge area from southern Anatolia to the Indian Ocean, and to approve an Arab caliphate. Hussein's point of view matters here because he claims to speak for "the whole of the Arab nation without any exception," which was a negotiating position, since not all Arabs actually followed him. He was trying to make his demands look as strong as possible so Britain would accept them. McMahon's reply in Document 2 says Britain will "recognise and support the independence of the Arabs," but he adds caveats, excluding land west of Damascus, Homs, Hama and Aleppo and only acting where Britain was "free to act without detriment to the interests of her ally, France." McMahon's purpose was to win Arab support in the war without upsetting France, so his language was left vague on purpose. Based on these promises, Hussein's sons led the Arab Revolt in 1916, attacking Ottoman forces and the Hejaz railway with British help, which shows Arabs actually acted to gain authority for themselves.

However, at the same time Britain was making a different deal. The Sykes-Picot Agreement in Document 3 does mention "independent Arab states," but it gives France and Britain the right to supply advisers in areas A and B and to set up "direct or indirect administration or control" in the blue and red zones. The map in Document 4 shows this clearly, with the blue area along the Syrian coast, the red area around Baghdad and Basra, and the signatures of Sykes and Picot. This agreement was secret until the Russian revolutionaries published it in 1917, so Arab leaders did not know about it when they were fighting. Then in Document 5, the Balfour Declaration promises a "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine, which was another commitment that conflicted with what Arabs thought they were promised.

The peace settlement made European control official but in a new form. Article 22 of the League Covenant in Document 6 says some peoples are "not yet able to stand by themselves" and should be under the "tutelage" of "advanced nations." This paternalist language was written by the winning powers and made their control sound like a duty instead of imperialism. It does say former Turkish communities could be "provisionally recognized" as independent, but only with a Mandatory's advice. In practice France got Syria and Lebanon, and Britain got Iraq and Palestine. When Faisal tried to rule an Arab government in Damascus, the French defeated his forces at Maysalun in 1920 and took control.

Still, Arab demands did not disappear and they shaped the new order. Britain made Faisal king of Iraq in 1921, after a revolt there, so Arab rulers did hold some authority even under the mandates. Palestine was different, though. In Document 7, the 1922 White Paper answers the Arab delegation and denies that Britain ever promised "an independent national government" in Palestine. This shows the disagreement over what McMahon meant in Document 2. Overall, political authority changed a lot because new states and rulers appeared, but real power mostly moved from the Ottomans to Britain and France.

Between 1200 and 1750 the movement of goods, ideas, and diseases along long-distance trade networks changed a lot, mostly because the Americas were added to the networks after 1492. However, some things stayed the same, because trade in Asia and Africa kept going along the old routes.

The Mongols were important in the early part of this period. They conquered a huge part of Eurasia in the 1200s, which made the Silk Road safer for merchants to travel on.

One example of change is the Columbian Exchange. After Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, new crops and animals moved between the Americas and the Eastern Hemisphere. Potatoes and maize went to Europe and Asia, and horses and cattle went to the Americas. Diseases like smallpox also came to the Americas and killed a very large share of the native people there. This was a big change because the two hemispheres had never been connected like this before, so the networks became truly global.

Another example is the Black Death in the 1300s. It spread along trade routes across Asia and reached Europe in the late 1340s, and it killed many people. This shows that trade networks carried diseases even before 1492, so disease moving along trade routes was also a continuity. The plague spread along the Silk Road and the Mediterranean ports, and it hurt the population of cities that were connected by trade.

Ideas also moved along the networks. Islam spread through merchants along the Indian Ocean trade and into West Africa and Southeast Asia. This kept happening in the whole period, so religion spreading with merchants did not really change.

Overall, the biggest change was the Americas joining the networks, which brought new crops and diseases and also silver. But the Indian Ocean and the Silk Road still carried spices, silk, and other goods like they did before. So the networks changed in size but kept many of their older patterns.

input.essay:
Between 1200 and 1750 long-distance trade networks changed a lot in their scale and reach, mainly because the Americas were connected to Afro-Eurasia after 1492 and European maritime empires used new ship technology to join existing routes. However, the change was not complete, because much of the trade in Asia and the Indian Ocean was still run by Asian and African merchants, and religions and diseases kept spreading along older routes the way they had before. So the networks changed more in size than in their basic structure, at least until the later part of the period.

Before 1200 there were already big trade networks. The Indian Ocean trade depended on the monsoon winds, which let merchants sail one direction in one season and come back in another. Muslim merchants spread Islam to East African cities like Kilwa and to parts of Southeast Asia through this trade. In the 13th century the Mongols conquered a huge empire from China to Eastern Europe, and the Pax Mongolica made the Silk Roads safer for merchants and travelers like Marco Polo. This mattered because it made exchange faster across Eurasia, which set up both more trade and the spread of disease.

One continuity is that diseases traveled along trade routes. In the 1340s the Black Death spread from Central Asia along Mongol-controlled routes and then by sea to the Mediterranean, killing roughly a third of Europe's population. The same pattern of disease following trade happened after 1492, but on a much bigger scale. In the Columbian Exchange, smallpox and other diseases from Europe killed a huge share of the Native American population because they had no immunity. This shows continuity because disease still followed the movement of people and goods, but it is also a change because the effects were far worse and they fell mostly on one side of the exchange.

Goods also show a mix of change and continuity. The Columbian Exchange brought crops like potatoes and maize to Afro-Eurasia, and horses, cattle, and sugar to the Americas. This was new because these crops had never moved between hemispheres before, and it led to population growth in places like China. Silver from Potosi in the Andes was shipped across the Pacific on the Manila galleons to China, which wanted silver for its economy. This created the first truly global trade network. But China was still at the center of demand like it had been before, and Europeans mostly used American silver to buy Asian goods like silk and porcelain, so Asian production stayed important.

Ideas spread in both old and new ways. Islam kept spreading through merchants in the Indian Ocean, and Mansa Musa's hajj in 1324 showed how West Africa was linked to the Islamic world through trans-Saharan trade in gold. After 1500, Christianity spread in a newer way, through missionaries who came with empires, like the Spanish in Mexico and the Jesuits in Asia. In the Americas this was spread more by force and conquest than Islam had been in Southeast Asia, but in places like Japan and China missionaries had little success, which shows Europeans did not control everything.

Also, the Atlantic slave trade moved millions of enslaved Africans to the Americas to work on sugar plantations. Slavery and slave trading existed before, but the size and racial basis of this trade was a major change.

In conclusion, long-distance exchange changed a great deal in scale between 1200 and 1750 because of the Columbian Exchange and European sea empires, but many older patterns, such as Asian merchants, the spread of Islam through trade, and diseases following routes, continued.

(A) The authors claim that European nations used military force to open sustained trade with China on their own terms, beginning with the Opium War. After that, China was compelled to sign a series of unequal treaties that let foreigners set up essentially autonomous economic bases and operate with privileged status inside China.

(B) The Treaty of Nanjing (1842), and the supplementary treaty with Britain signed the next year, support this claim. The treaty gave Hong Kong to Britain, opened five treaty ports including Shanghai and Canton, and set low fixed tariffs that China could not change. The 1843 supplement granted extraterritoriality, so British subjects in China were tried in their own consular courts instead of Chinese courts, and a most-favored-nation clause meant any privilege later given to another power automatically went to Britain too. This created the kind of privileged, semi-autonomous foreign presence the authors describe.

(C) China and Japan were similar at first because both were forced into unequal treaties. After Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853-54, Japan signed treaties that opened ports and gave Westerners extraterritoriality and fixed tariffs, just like China. The big difference is how each country responded. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japan centralized power and industrialized quickly, got rid of extraterritoriality by 1899, and defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95. Qing self-strengthening was limited by conservative officials and a weak central government, so China kept losing territory and sovereignty, for example by giving up Taiwan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki.
